fixes.explanation: Loyalty is the word. Abraham tells Abimelech what he asked of Sarah: “This is how you can show your loyalty to me…” (Genesis 20:13) He's explaining himself to the king after the fact. He ties the request to when God had him journey from his father's house.

That's what Abraham says of his wife Sarah while he's staying in Gerar (Genesis 20:2). Four little words, and this chapter is off and running. Abimelech, king of Gerar, is about to hear them, and I think things are about to get complicated for him.

Abraham never calls Sarah his servant here. The text says he said of his wife, “She is my sister.” (Genesis 20:2) Servant is a very different word to use about your wife, friend. Sister is the one he actually says.
The text doesn't have Abimelech sending Abraham anywhere. What it says is that Abimelech had Sarah brought to him (Genesis 20:2). His move is about Sarah, not about getting rid of Abraham.

No prison shows up anywhere in this passage. Abimelech's move is to have Sarah brought to him (Genesis 20:2). Abraham is never locked up. Later Abimelech gives him sheep, cattle, menservants and maidservants (Genesis 20:14), and I think that's a strange gift to hand a prisoner.

God tells Abimelech, “You are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken, for she is a married woman.” (Genesis 20:3) That's a heavy thing to hear, even in a dream. I bet Abimelech's eyes were wide open the whole time he was asleep.

God says Abraham “…is a prophet…” (Genesis 20:7). God names him that right alongside the order to return the man's wife. What that means here shows up in the next words: Abraham will pray for Abimelech, and Abimelech will live.

God doesn't use servant in this verse. He says Abraham “…is a prophet…” (Genesis 20:7). That's the title God gives him, and it comes right before God says Abraham will pray for Abimelech so that he lives.
Abimelech isn't talking about money here. His words are “…such tremendous guilt upon me and my kingdom?” (Genesis 20:9) I think that word tells you how heavy it feels to him.

Abraham says, “Surely there is no fear of God in this place.” (Genesis 20:11) That's what he tells Abimelech he thought to himself. He follows it with, “They will kill me on account of my wife.” (Genesis 20:11) So the worry he names is about his own life.

Altar isn't the word Abraham uses. He says, “Surely there is no fear of God in this place.” (Genesis 20:11) He's talking about what he thought was in the people of Gerar, not what they had built. You can't check for fear of God by counting furniture, friend.

Abraham doesn't say love. His words are “Surely there is no fear of God in this place.” (Genesis 20:11) That's what he tells Abimelech he thought to himself, and fear of God is the thing he says he didn't expect to find. Then he adds, “They will kill me on account of my wife.” (Genesis 20:11)

Courage isn't what Abraham says. He asks Sarah, “This is how you can show your loyalty to me…” (Genesis 20:13) Loyalty is about sticking with him, not about being brave. The thing he asks her to say is that he's her brother, wherever they go.

Abimelech says, “Look, my land is before you. Settle wherever you please.” (Genesis 20:15) That's a wide-open invitation from a king. It comes right after he gives Abraham sheep, cattle and servants and restores Sarah to him (Genesis 20:14).

Abimelech doesn't talk about protection here. He tells Sarah, “It is your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared.” (Genesis 20:16) The silver is about clearing her name in front of everyone with her. Guarding her isn't what he says.
